response:
Complete Portfolio Website Analysis and Implementation Instructions

I've reviewed the full-page screenshot you shared earlier, including the enlarged views of the individual sections. This report covers the entire visible homepage, from the navigation bar to the contact section.

The website currently has a recognizable electrical-engineering identity: dark instrumentation panels, technical labels, signal-green accents, interactive engineering visualizations, and a system-oriented layout.

However, the primary issue is that the website looks like several independent engineering demonstrations arranged vertically, rather than one cohesive, immersive engineering portfolio.

The most important improvements are structural: better use of desktop space, stronger visual hierarchy, connected engineering diagrams, more substantial project presentations, and consistent relationships between visualizations and their underlying engineering concepts.

I'll provide implementation-level instructions that your coding agent can use directly. References to file paths and component names are illustrative; the agent should inspect the actual repository before making changes.

A full-page screenshot cannot confirm whether animations, interactive controls, navigation, or responsive breakpoints work correctly. I'll identify visible issues separately from functionality that requires browser testing.

1. Navigation
Current state

The navigation is positioned at the top of the page and contains a small personal logo, a group of primary navigation links, and a green availability indicator on the right.

The header is minimal and visually unobtrusive.

Its current design does not compete with the hero, but it also does not contribute much to the portfolio's intended instrumentation-inspired appearance.

Issue 1.1 — Navigation lacks a distinctive visual identity

The header resembles a conventional minimalist portfolio navigation bar.

The logo, navigation links, and availability indicator appear as separate elements rather than parts of a unified interface.

Fix instructions

Inspect the existing header component and identify how the logo, navigation links, and status indicator are positioned.

Use a consistent horizontal alignment system and shared spacing tokens.

Keep the header compact, but introduce a subtle engineering-inspired treatment.

For example, use a thin horizontal trace beneath the navigation links with a small illuminated indicator under the active destination.

The active indicator should move between links when the current route or section changes.

Do not introduce elaborate animations or redesign the entire header as a technical dashboard.

The intended result is a navigation bar that feels like part of the same engineered system as the rest of the website.

Issue 1.2 — Navigation typography appears very small

In the screenshot, the navigation labels have limited visual presence.

Some apparent smallness is caused by the full-page screenshot being compressed, so actual computed font sizes need to be checked.

Fix instructions

Inspect the navigation at its original desktop viewport.

Use approximately 12–14 px as an initial target for uppercase navigation labels.

Keep letter spacing restrained.

Ensure that the labels remain clearly readable against the dark background.

Use slightly stronger contrast for active and hovered links without making inactive links nearly invisible.

Check that increasing text size does not cause the navigation to overlap the availability indicator.

Issue 1.3 — The availability indicator appears disconnected

The green availability indicator sits on the far right but has little visual relationship with the rest of the navigation.

Fix instructions

Treat the availability indicator as a deliberate status component.

Align it vertically with the navigation links.

Use a consistent green status dot and readable text.

If the indicator animates, keep the movement subtle and disable it for reduced-motion preferences.

Do not present the indicator as live availability unless the displayed status is actually maintained.

Issue 1.4 — Responsive navigation needs verification

The screenshot does not show the mobile navigation state.

Fix instructions

Test the header at 1440, 1024, 768, and 390 px viewport widths.

At smaller widths, verify that navigation links do not overlap or overflow.

Use the existing mobile navigation implementation if one is already present.

The mobile menu must provide visible focus states, keyboard operation, accessible labels, and a clear close action.

If the header is sticky, verify that navigating to a section does not position its heading underneath the header.

Apply scroll-margin-top to section targets where necessary.

2. Hero section
Current state

The hero contains your name in large white typography, followed by your professional title, supporting technical information, an introductory statement, and an Explore Systems CTA.

Nearly all the meaningful content is positioned on the left.

The rest of the hero is predominantly empty.

The typography provides a recognizable personal identity, but the section does not yet establish the visual character of the engineering systems showcased further down the page.

Primary visual problem
The hero feels incomplete because its composition is dominated by unused space.

The text establishes who you are, but the surrounding visual environment does not sufficiently communicate the engineering work that makes the portfolio distinctive.

Issue 2.1 — Excessive unused space on the right

The hero is visually unbalanced.

The right side has no clearly recognizable visual centerpiece, while the left side contains the name and nearly all the supporting content.

Fix instructions

Inspect the hero container's width, grid structure, and alignment.

Establish a deliberate two-part desktop composition.

Use the left portion for your identity, engineering statement, and CTA.

Use the right portion for one substantial engineering visualization derived from your actual work.

A reasonable starting layout is:

CSS
.hero-layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 0.9fr) minmax(0, 1.1fr);
  align-items: center;
  gap: clamp(2rem, 5vw, 6rem);
}

The exact proportions should be adjusted after inspecting the rendered result.

The engineering visualization should not be a generic glowing PCB, random particle field, or decorative collection of electrical symbols.

It should represent something meaningful, such as a real system architecture, an actual hardware design, or a signal moving between recognizable engineering subsystems.

Preserve the current typography as the hero's primary identity element.

The engineering visual should complement the text rather than compete with it.

Issue 2.2 — The introductory statement lacks prominence

The statement about building systems where hardware, software, and signals meet appears relatively small beneath the name.

That statement is important because it connects your different engineering disciplines.

Fix instructions

Establish three distinct typography levels.

The primary level is your name.

The secondary level is the central engineering statement.

The tertiary level contains your professional title, disciplines, and supporting metadata.

Increase the prominence of the engineering statement while keeping it clearly subordinate to your name.

Do not simply enlarge every line of text.

Use line lengths and spacing that make the statement feel intentional.

Issue 2.3 — The hero does not visibly establish the global signal system

Your original implementation concept is based on a signal traveling through the website.

In the screenshot, the hero does not clearly establish where this signal begins.

The Engineering Network appears to introduce a separate visual element rather than continuing something established in the hero.

Fix instructions

Create a clearly defined signal source inside the hero visualization.

The signal should travel through the hero and terminate at a deliberate connection point near the transition into the next section.

Align this endpoint with the incoming signal path in the Engineering Network.

Use one shared set of visual conventions for signal width, color, node appearance, and direction.

The connection does not have to be one enormous SVG covering the entire document.

Separate responsive SVG sections can share a consistent visual endpoint and scroll-progress state.

The important requirement is that the transition appears continuous to the visitor.

Issue 2.4 — The hero's final animation state may be underdeveloped

The screenshot shows the completed hero composition but little of the intended powered-system atmosphere.

This does not establish that the boot animation is broken.

However, the final state should remain visually complete even when no animation is playing.

Fix instructions

Inspect the initial animation, intermediate states, and final rendered state.

Ensure that the primary content is not hidden behind a prolonged boot sequence.

The visual centerpiece should remain visible after the sequence finishes.

The CTA should remain accessible throughout or become available promptly.

When reduced motion is enabled, render the completed hero state directly.

Do not rely on animation to make an otherwise incomplete layout feel impressive.

Issue 2.5 — Mobile hero composition needs a dedicated layout

The desktop composition should not simply shrink into two narrow columns on mobile.

Fix instructions

At the appropriate breakpoint, change the hero to a single-column layout.

Keep your name and professional identity prominent.

Place the engineering visual beneath or partially behind the text only if readability remains intact.

Reduce the visualization's complexity if necessary.

Avoid forcing the mobile visitor to scroll through an oversized decorative visual before reaching the next section.

3. Engineering Network
Current state

The Engineering Network contains a bright green signal trace near the top of the section.

Several engineering-domain labels are distributed below it.

The trace has a clean electrical appearance, but the composition does not clearly establish how the individual domains connect.

The main trace appears separated from much of the network.

The surrounding labels are small and scattered across a comparatively large region.

This section needs a structural redesign of its visual composition rather than another isolated alignment adjustment.

Issue 3.1 — The signal trace and domain nodes appear disconnected

The existing trace is visually prominent, but the nodes beneath it do not appear to form a complete connected system.

Fix instructions

Inspect the SVG path definitions, coordinate system, and node-positioning implementation.

Identify where the main trace is intended to connect to each domain.

Create a complete network topology before adjusting individual CSS positions.

The resulting architecture should establish an identifiable signal input, meaningful branches, connected domain nodes, and a continuation toward the next section.

For example, the network might use a central system node connected to embedded systems, FPGA, sensors, power, and control.

Do not create arbitrary technical relationships
